newsitem.title: USA: Koop warns of flaws in tobacco deal.
newsitem.headline: Koop warns of flaws in tobacco deal.

text.p: Former U.S. Surgeon General C. Everett Koop warned on Saturday there were serious flaws in Friday's landmark tobacco agreement between states and cigarette makers.
And he described as "paltry" the $368.5 billion tobacco companies agreed to pay over 25 years in a settlement with the 40 states which had sued them for health care costs.
In a CNN interview Koop said he feared the agreement would be watered down on Capitol Hill and that tobacco industry lawyers would find loopholes to exploit.

"It's a big concern for all those of us who worked three decades with the tobacco industry and find you can't trust them. I am sure they will take every effort they can to find the loopholes," said Koop.

A fierce opponent of the tobacco industry who succeeded in forcing health warnings to be put on cigarette packets, Koop said the agreement was far from being a great triumph for the attorneys general, health advocates and the anti-tobacco lobby.

"They are talking about it as a marvelous achievement. I would put it in the sense of a marvelous effort. The achievement is yet to come," he said. "Whether that effort becomes an achievement depends a lot on Congress."

"Congress is open to the usual lobbying by the tobacco industry and they have always been very partial to the tobacco industry, so I think a tremendous number of things can be watwered down in Congress which will not be good for the health of the American people," he said.
"When we look back on it five years from now it will be a much smaller agreement than what was presented to us by the attorneys general yesterday," Koop added.
Koop said many of the aspects of the deal that were good for children might be negated by "what is a very serious flaw in the agreement."

His major concern was a new provision on the Food and Drug Administration's powers to reduce nicotine in cigarettes, which he described as impossible to meet as the FDA would have to prove a significant reduction in health effects.
Also, any request for a change by cigarette manufacturers had to be technically feasible.
"That is a reasonable request, but for all other industries the FDA sets the standards and industry makes its feasible," he said. "Here the FDA has to take care of feasibility."
An agreement that there could be no change in cigarette manufacture if there was any chance of a contraband reaction -- smuggling or black market -- was a major stumbling block.

"This is a negative thing that's almost impossible to prove and requires most scrutiny by Congress and the White House," he said. "It's like removing and end run and pass for making forward progress."
Koop was also critical of the $368.5 billion the tobacco companies agreed to pay in return for immunity from further punitive liability for any past deception, fraud or conspiracy.

"Money to the tobacco industry is not important. They can make up anything they give away by just increasing the price of cigarettes. When you break down various things they offered per death and per pack of cigarettes, the amount is paltry," he said.
